chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Ismail, from Mansur ibn Yunus, from Muhammad al-Halby, who said:

I was sitting in the presence of a judge among the judges, and Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) was sitting with him. Two men came to him, and one of them said: 'I hired the camel of this man to carry my goods to one of the mines. I stipulated upon him that he bring me into the mine on such and such a day, because it is a market day, and I fear I might miss it. So if he were to detain me from that, I would deduct from the hire charge for each day he detains me, such and such an amount. And indeed, he detained me from that time for such and such days.' The judge said: 'This is an invalid stipulation; pay him his full hire charge.' When the man arose, Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) turned to me and said: 'This stipulation of his is valid, as long as he does not deduct the entirety of his hire charge.'

key_terms.إِبِلَ: Camels (plural of camel, used here for the animal/service)
key_terms.تَكَارَيْتُ: I hired (verb from kira, hire charge)

ai.seo_question: Is a conditional penalty clause valid in an Islamic hiring contract according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith highlights the jurisprudential distinction between the Imam and the contemporary Qadi regarding conditional stipulations (shurut) in Ijarah contracts, emphasizing that partial deductions are permissible provided they do not amount to total forfeiture of the wage. It underscores the Shia scholarly principle of facilitating commercial transactions by validating flexible terms that reflect actual service duration or utility, rather than imposing rigid penalties. This ruling aligns with the broader legal maxim that conditions in contracts are valid unless they contradict the essence of the contract or cause undue hardship.
